title.narrative: Carter Center -Stöd till demokratisk styrning och mänskliga rättigheter
The Carter Center - Advancing Democratic Governance & Respect for HR/2017-2019

description.narrative: Insatsen ska bidra till att nå målen för Sveriges strategi för utvecklingssamarbete i DRK 2015-2019 och då speciellt området - Stärkt kapacitet i det civila samhället att verka för öppenhet, ansvarsutkrävande och ökad respekt för mänskliga rättigheter. Insatsen uppgår till 30 mkr för en 3 -årsperiod och Carter Center (TCC) är genomförare. TCC ska arbeta för att stärka det civila samhället i DRK i sin roll att övervaka och rapportera om mänskliga rättigheter, gruvnäringen och politiska val samt att ta fram underlag till kampanjer inom dessa områden. TCC ska stärka civila samhällsorganisationer att nå ut till marginaliserade grupper, stärka ungdomsorganisationer samt stärka nämnda organisationers interna kapacitet inom t ex intern styrning och kontroll.

The Carter Center (TCC) has applied to Sida for funding of 30 million SEK to carry out the “ Advancing democratic governance and respect for human rights in the DRC” project during the period 2017-2020. The intervention aims at : 1) Improved monitoring, analysis, and reporting 2) Enhanced advocacy for reform 3) Increased community engagement 4) Strengthened organisational capacity The organisation implementing the intervention is The Carter Center. The project is fully financed by Sweden, it is based on TCCs country program, but TCC itself allocates also internal resources for its implementation. Other donors are also funding TCCs work in DRC in similar areas, based on TCCs country program. The budget is divided with: 7 000 000 SEK for the year 2017 13 000 000 SEK for the year 2018 10 000 000 SEK for the year 2019 The project will target Congolese Human Rights CSOs, Young civil society leaders and extractive industries. Sweden has previously supported TCCs work in the DRC with app. 30 MSEK for 2013-2106. An external evaluation of this support was undertaken in 2016 showing positive outcomes.

The programme describes how TCC intends to advance democratic governance and respect of human rights as well strengthen youth political participation in the DRC. It also describes objectives and proposed results, mainly focused on the better understanding of the democratic process, motoring of natural resources, capacity of women and youth leaders and activists to engage in democratic debate and to improve resilience in managing security threats, especially during the electoral period.

The collaboration with TCC enabled most partners of the SIDA-funded program to grow their sector specific technical expertise and be recognized as experts in their fields by others, develop internal management mechanisms, and access alternative sources of funding. The present concluding assessments summarize a number of common dimensions where capacities were strengthened, and further elaborates on specific success story aspects of result outcomes. Across all three component (Extractive Industry, Election and Human Rights monitoring), TCC coached partners on how to develop internal tools and methodologies, related to either technical dimensions or organizational aspects. Final evaluation report found that these internal documents were important outputs, and strong indicators that capacities were effectively strengthened. They fall either into the organizational capacity development cluster (objective 4) or the monitoring, analysis, and reporting efforts (objective 1). Regarding Election: several planning documents developed in the context of the election observation mission contributed to the overall structuring of Justice and Peace Commission (JPC) at catholic church as an organization. This included a human resources policy which was also comprised of planning tools for the selection, hiring, training and deployment of over 40,000 observers, both short and long term , an internal and external communications policy, as well as a gender policy. On specific substantive issues, an advocacy strategy for electoral reform was also elaborated by JPC. Similarly, the Human Rights House (HRH) program saw the development of new documents such as strategic plans, communications plans, a fundraising guide and an internal procedures manual a.k.a. code of conduct among some of its partners.
The EIG component introduced innovative methodologies with its CSO partners, including the Human Rights Impact Assessment (HRIA), a participatory action-research tool to evaluating the effects of extractive projects on communities; and the Social Expenditure Index (SEI), a methodology to assess the performance of community development project aimed at mitigating the negative impact of extractive operations, using evaluation criteria akin to the OECD DAC evaluation framework. Additional information on HRIA and SEI is available on page 18 of year 3 programme report. Further important evidence of the improvement in CSO partners capacities is their ability to compile and analyse the data they collected into well-crafted publications, especially reports. These public documents have become, in a manner of speaking, the calling card of the CSOs vis-à-vis the outside world. Several beneficiary testimonies have indicated their appreciation for the quality of those reports. As part of programme M&E framework, it is notable that JPC observation reports covered not only electoral operations surrounding election day, but also a series of pre-electoral matters. The programs performance indicators at outcome and objective levels are yet another body of information which attests to CSOs improved capacities. According to the final aggregated data of the Results Assessment Framework, almost all outcome-level targets were reached, while most indicators have actually largely surpassed the intended target. The two targets that were not reached quality of reports and observation data reported by female observers fell only one percentage point below the objective. Members of partner CSOs have become well-respected experts in the Election sector, they have learnt that evidence-based investigations are powerful tools to pass messages across and have become relevant interlocutors of the mining industry and the government. They are now assertively contributing to the expert debate on governance, transparency, and human rights. We were also told that some women who followed the TCC trainings do not fear anymore to ask questions or raise points even in front of large gatherings (of men). As indicated earlier, trained CSOs are produced good quality reports on fiscal and human rights impact assessment case studies, have increased their knowledge on HRIA theory, methodology, and social expenditures research. Today, CSOs make their own analysis and publish independent reports. Strong expertise was developed by CSOs in assessing community development projects thanks to a step-bystep participative approach. 50 projects implemented by 13 mining companies were evaluated in five provinces. The use of Human Rights Impact Assessment (HRIA) tools triggered the interest of the Senior Advisor in charge of Poverty Alleviation from the office of the DRC President, Mr. Judée Badibanga. He contacted TCC to find ways to operationalize the reports methodology and recommendations. The intensive field work allowed as well to document the poor results of most of the social responsibility projects implemented by mining companies (very high costs, projects not adapted to needs, unsustainable, no respect of construction standards). The direct observation of abuses on human rights (no fair compensation for relocation, negative impact on the environment, pollutions affecting the health of communities) have highlighted important flaws of the mining industry and led to changes in policy and practice (more information on these changes on page 21 program final evaluation report). Despite the good results mentioned above, it was found that some CSOs could benefit from further support, particularly in the field of selecting more independent community representatives involved in the discussion process with mining companies over the Cahier des Charges. Strong community leaders apparently managed to influence the respective CSO in its choices in two particular cases, which triggered tensions among community members. The latter felt that their interests were not properly represented. The mining company would have appreciated a closer support of TCC to the CSO in charge of the community dialogue, as it was allegedly lacking the necessary skills to implement a smooth negotiation process and was rather contributing, possibly inadvertently, to increase tensions. There was also a mining company representative who stated that TCC should bring more support to the CSO that investigated their site, as he felt that it was looking for weaknesses only, and did not give him the opportunity to explain what measures have been put in place to mitigate the well-known problems. This statement needs of course to be further investigated as we got only one perspective of the situation. It should as well be reminded that TCCs methodology includes the opportunity for mining companies to provide information in the research phase and to respond to specific issues identified in the course of the assessment. And finally, because the topic of HRIA is highly technical, some CSOs mentioned that although they tremendously increased their knowledge thanks to very well-designed training modules, or got specific technical assistance, they would appreciate to have further support in these aspects. GIZ took partly over from TCC and further funded directly some CSOs to work specifically on the Cahier des Charges.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
